WEDNESDAY, 27 OCTOBER 2010
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
Financial Statements, Crown—Trends
1. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East) to the Minister of Finance:
What trends are evident in the Government’s latest financial statements?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The financial statements for the year
ended 30 June 2010 show that the Government is generally on track with its fiscal
management. The fact that core Crown expenses were flat at $64 billion from one year
to the next indicates we are getting on top of expenditure control. The residual cash
deficit increased slightly, from $8.6 billion to $9 billion for the year ended in June. This
deficit is forecast to rise to $13.3 billion for the 2010-11 financial year.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What trends in net Crown debt were highlighted in the
Government’s latest annual accounts?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Net Crown debt is increasing as the Government absorbs the
shock of the recent recession on its own books, helping to protect New Zealanders from
the sharp edges of that recession. Core Crown debt is now around $27 billion, or just
over 14 percent of GDP. That debt will continue to rise, because this year the
Government expects there will be a cash deficit of around $13 billion. However, we
cannot keep running deficits or increasing debt forever, and that is why the Government
has a 5 or 6-year track towards a surplus, involving tight control of Government
spending.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Can he tell hard-working Kiwis why he has borrowed an extra
three-quarters of a billion dollars in the last 2 months to pay for his economic
mismanagement?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. Fortunately, a lot of hard-working Kiwis understand just
how much this Government needs to do to correct the economic mismanagement of the
previous Government and to deal with the recession. That is why the Government’s
economic policies are broadly supported.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What do the latest forecasts show about the likely path for the
economy and the Government’s finances?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Treasury is currently working on forecasts, which will be
published at the half-year update on 14 December. As I told the Finance and
Expenditure Committee today, tax receipts for July and August were lower than
forecast. I am told that the September tax receipts are up a bit, clawing back some of the
difference. It is difficult to draw detailed conclusions from just 2 or 3 months’ worth of
data, but I would expect that in the half-year update tax revenue will be a bit softer, and
that may flow through to the rest of the Government accounts.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What positive signs is he seeing from the nature of the current
economic recovery?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, many—many positive signs. As we have talked about
in the House, this economy needs to be rebalanced away from excessive property
speculation, excessive Government spending, and excessive personal consumption. The
early signs of the recovery are promising. Private consumption is pretty much flat,
because New Zealanders are saving a good deal more than they were. Although that has
14844 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Oct 2010
meant a more muted economic recovery in the short term, it is laying a stronger
platform for sustainable economic recovery in the long term.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Why did he tell the Finance and Expenditure Committee today
that there was “no V-shaped recovery”, when the Prime Minister said it would be
aggressive; and who is right: he and the Governor of the Reserve Bank, who think the
recovery is slow and fragile, or his boss, whom he describes as floating from cloud to
cloud?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As we have gone over this issue about 10 times in the House
and the select committee, I will explain it again. The Prime Minister made his
comments in early 2009, and he was correct; the economy turned round from a 2.5
percent contraction to about a 2 percent growth rate. Like other developed economies,
as New Zealand households have increased their savings dramatically, it has meant that
they have less to spend. That is why retailers and the construction industry are finding it
tough.
Economic Policies—Contribution to Medium-term Fiscal Consolidation
2. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister of Finance: Is he
satisfied that all the Government’s economic policies contribute to the goal of “clear,
credible, ambitious and growth-friendly, medium-term fiscal consolidation”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The answer to that is yes. The goal
the member is referring to is one that was set out either by the OECD or the G20
finance Ministers in their recent communiqué.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How does it help to meet this goal by paying over $1 billion a year in
accommodation supplement subsidies to landlords, especially as the total Government
housing subsidy is expected to rise to nearly $3 billion by 2016?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will be aware there has been debate for some
time about what drives the cost of housing. We will continue to pay the accommodation
supplement to tenants. I know some believe that that is just passed on to landlords, but
they should try taking it off the tenants and see what happens. Of course, it would leave
them in an unacceptable situation. The member will know that the Government has
done a review of State housing, and a number of our Resource Management Act
changes are designed to increase the supply of affordable housing.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does he agree, then, that it is an inadequate supply of housing to
meet the current deficit of 70,000 homes that is fuelling the projected blowout of the
Government’s housing subsidy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think the member is probably at least in part right that
constraints on the supply of housing drive up the cost of housing, including for those
tenants that the Government is subsidising. I look forward to the Green Party’s support
of the changes the Government is making to our regulatory structures to improve the
supply of affordable housing.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister, then, consider a State house building programme
like that proposed in the Green Party’s Mind the Gap package of 6,000 homes over 3 to
5 years, which will help to address the housing shortage, constrain the growth in the
housing subsidy, and create 28,000 jobs in the process?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government’s obvious preference would be that the
private sector was able to expand the supply of affordable houses. We have just done a
review of State housing, where a pretty broad-based group with a lot of experience in
housing made the point that the simple growth in the number of State houses often does
not help those who are most in need. They are the Government’s priority.
27 Oct 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 14845

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why, then, is the Government prepared to borrow ever-increasing
sums of money to fund a housing subsidy for landlords, yet is not prepared to borrow to
invest in building homes for New Zealand families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am not sure whether we are disagreeing here. The
Government would like to see a greater supply of affordable housing. It is somewhat
ironic, though, that the Green Party is among those who most vociferously object to
new subdivisions and to the expansion of housing. If we could get those rules changed
in local bodies so as to encourage more affordable housing, then that might drop the
cost of the rental subsidy, as well as increase the opportunities for first-home buyers.
Parity with Australia—Progress
3. Hon PHIL GOFF (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: What
recent progress has he made on catching up with Australia?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister) on behalf of the Prime Minister:
In terms of catching up with Australia, the biggest step we have taken is to return the
economy to growth after five quarters of economic contraction, which started under the
previous Labour Government. The second-biggest step we have taken is to start undoing
the damage done by the wrong-headed economic policy of the previous Labour
Government. As the member will know, the Australian economy did not go into
recession at all, so we have been starting from some way behind.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: How many net additional jobs does he expect to see created in New
Zealand this year compared with the quarter of a million new, net additional jobs that
Australia has, so far, created this year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I cannot give the member that number, but I can say that as
Australia has had its terms of trade double in 5 years because of the value of its resource
base, up against our commodities, whose terms of trade have increased by about 50
percent, then of course there will be a challenge. Equally, we had a recession and
Australia did not. That member’s party might be able to explain why New Zealand went
into recession under his Government, before the global financial crisis, and Australia
did not.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Will the first decline in the median income in New Zealand to take
place in more than a decade, which Statistics New Zealand recorded over the last year,
help close the income gap with Australia?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: When the member was away we discussed in the House how
useless the median income measure is, because it does not measure what happens to
household incomes. That member ought to explain how the Labour Government
managed to drive New Zealand into recession when the Australian economy did not go
into recession. He was in the Government at the time.

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: How have wages in New Zealand fallen behind those in Australia?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The history of this is quite interesting. Between September
1999 and September 2008 real after-tax wages in New Zealand rose only 3 percent. In
contrast, in the same period in Australia, real after-tax wages rose 19 percent. So over
the last decade wages in New Zealand fell a long way behind wages in Australia. Since
that time, I am happy to say, we have made progress towards reducing the wage gap,
but it is early days yet.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: When will the unemployment rate in New Zealand, which has
reached nearly one in two for Māori and Pasifika teenage girls and over one in three for
Māori and Pasifika teenage boys, persuade him that he needs to give the same priority
and focus to skill training and education to our young people at risk instead of cutting,
as he did last week, $55 million out of skill training?
14846 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Oct 2010

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member may not be aware that about 100,000 people
who are participating in the industry training system were getting no credits whatsoever.
With the agreement of the industry training sector, the Government has taken the
unutilised and wasted money and shifted it to where it can be more usefully employed.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: When putting together his tax package, what consideration did he
give to ensuring that most of the benefit went to those on modest incomes, as they did in
Australia, rather than the lion’s share of the benefit going to those on the top incomes,
as it does in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member is simply wrong, and the fact that he repeats
that description and includes Australia does not mean that he is right. The Government
published all the analysis in respect of the equity of the tax cuts after the Budget, and it
showed that when we take into account the impact of the increased taxes on property
and on foreign owners of New Zealand assets, the major income groups all got about
the same positive increase in income. That is the analysis and in fact no one has
challenged it.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Which of the policies introduced by his Government has done the
most to widen the income gap with Australia?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As we pointed out, the real after-tax wage gap has actually
closed. That is the measure that is used, and it was legislated by the previous
Government as the wage measure that is relative to national superannuation. We believe
that our whole raft of policies, including our investment in infrastructure,
microeconomic reform, our tax switch, our reform of the public sector, our focus on
education and skills, and our extension of innovation and business support are all
adding up to a policy that will close the gap with Australia.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Has he passed the test that he set for himself to close the gap with
Australia; or was that promise about as credible as his promise not to increase GST?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes. Our policies do pass the test. We have put together a
six-point economic programme, which we are executing. Ours is a programme that his
new friend Mrs Gillard would recognise, because she gave a speech a lot like ours, and
his policies are heading in the opposite direction from where his new friend Mrs Gillard
is going.
Gambling, Problem—Intervention Services
4. TE URUROA FLAVELL (Māori Party—Waiariki) to the Associate Minister
of Health: He aha ngā rautaki ka kōkuhua ki te whakautu i te pikinga mā te 25 ōrau o
ngā kiritaki hei whakararu nei i ngā ratonga aukati peti moni, otirā, tērā pikihanga e
5,325 i te tau 2008 ki te e 6,673 i te tau 2009; ā, ka whakaae a ia ki tā Barbara Phillips,
kaiwhakahaere nō te Manatū Hauora i kī rā “those seeking help are only a small
proportion of overall gambling prevalence”?
[What strategies have been introduced to respond to the 25 percent increase in
numbers of clients presenting to problem gambling intervention services, which rose
from 5,325 in 2008 to 6,673 in 2009; and does he agree with Ministry of Health
manager Barbara Phillips that “those seeking help are only a small proportion of
overall gambling prevalence”?]

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: The Government recently
approved a new 6-year strategy for the period 2010-16, and a funding plan for the
period 2010-30, including a comprehensive needs analysis based on client user statistics
such as the ones that the member has quoted, prevalence data, and models of best
practice. The 3-year service plan continues to provide for a range of services from
public health activity through to brief and comprehensive interventions. For
communities that do not have access to face-to-face services, the toll-free gambling
27 Oct 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 14847
helpline service is now available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Typically, clients
present to services in crisis, which is a smaller percentage of those affected by problem
gambling. The Government has therefore strengthened its focus on early interventions
in order to reach people before they reach that crisis point.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Kua hōparangia e te Minita o te Hauora ngā painga o te tuitui i te
kāri whai-pūtea me te kāri whakatū-whakapaunga-pūtea ki te rautaki whakakore
petipeti; ki te kore, he aha?
[Has the Minister of Health investigated the promotion of player tracking cards and
pre-commit cards as part of the integrated problem-gambling strategy; if not, why not?]

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I think a more logical comparison would be to look at data
from the same quarters of previous years. An analysis of Department of Internal Affairs
data shows that there continues to be a decline in spend in the non-casino gaming-
machine sector. For example, in September 2008 the sector spend was $232.3 million;
that fell to $220.7 million for the September 2009 quarter, and to $215.2 million for the
September 2010 quarter. I think that data provides the answers to the member’s
question.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: He āwangawanga ōna e pā ana ki ngā tatauranga e kī nei, ahakoa
kua mimiti te tokomaha o ngā raihana, ngā mihini petipeti me ngā whare petipeti i te tau
kua hipa, kua piki tonu te pūtea kua whakapauria i te hauwhā tau kua taha ake nei mai i
te $209m i te Pīpiri ki te $215m i te Here-turi-kōkā; ā, he aha ngā ara kei mua i te
tangata ki te whawhai i tēnei ngārara, te petipeti?
[Has he concerns that despite a decline in numbers of licence holders, gambling
venues, and gaming machines in the past year, spending in the last quarter still rose
from $209 million in June to $215 million in September; and what measures are in
place for a person to combat this addiction to gambling?]

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: The issue that the member raises falls within the
responsibility of the Department of Internal Affairs, but I am aware that we already
have systems that interrupt play on pokie machines that are known as pop-ups or player
information displays. I gather that some Australian states are proposing to implement
technology such as pre-commit cards, and I imagine that the Minister of Internal Affairs
would want to see the outcome of that move before determining whether to further
regulate the sector in New Zealand.
Child Poverty—Government Action
5. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour) to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development and Employment
items.text: What action, if any, has the Government taken to
reduce child poverty in New Zealand?
Hon JUDITH COLLINS (Acting Minister of Social Development and
Employment): Apart from the great economic work being achieved by this
Government’s robust fiscal policies, the Ministry of Social Development has done a
great deal to help children and families in these tough economic conditions, including
the Job Support Scheme, ReStart payments, Job Ops, Community Max, Break Away
programmes, and the highly successful Community Response Fund. In addition, we
have increased the abatement rate for the domestic purposes benefit and the invalids
benefit so people can earn more while still receiving the benefit.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Has the Government made a commitment to end child poverty
in New Zealand; if so, what timetable has been set to achieve it?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: It would be great to be able to say that we could end
child poverty in New Zealand. Certainly, the previous Government had 9 years to do it,
and the best economic times to do it, but never achieved it.
14848 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Oct 2010

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Will she support the Every Child Counts call to establish a
cross-party group to address child poverty, and will she seek to convince the Prime
Minister that it should be established, given that he dismissed the idea when I raised it
with him in November last year?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Has she seen the report from the Child Poverty Action Group,
which states that before the election National made political capital out of a so-called
underclass in New Zealand, but since the election child poverty has become invisible;
and has she argued in Cabinet for priority to be given to end child poverty in this
country—a country that can afford millions for a building to have a party in, yet
children have to wait?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I have not seen the report from the Child Poverty Action
Group. I can, however, say that under the very best economic times that the previous
Labour Government inherited it was not able to end child poverty. We have inherited a
recession and we are doing a fantastic job.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Does she agree with the Prime Minister’s Chief Science
Adviser, Professor Peter Gluckman, who said that the Government is putting the money
in the wrong end, that investing in troubled teens is often too late, and that the first 6
years of life are critical; will she ensure that funding is provided to reduce child poverty,
even if she will not commit to ending it—reduce it as happened under the previous
Government—and will she commit to reducing it in the next Budget?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The best way out of poverty for families is work—
[Interruption] Well, I know that that might be a four-letter word for Labour members,
but it is not for this side. I agree with the Children’s Commissioner, who said that work
is a road to salvation.
Prisons—Staff Safety
6. SANDRA GOUDIE (National—Coromandel) to the Minister of Corrections:
What reports has she received on initiatives to improve the safety of prison staff?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The safety of Department of
Corrections officers is one of our top priorities, and I am very pleased to report that the
department has delivered an intensive 3-day training course in advanced tactical
communication and de-escalation techniques to its entire front-line staff of 4,000. This
was delivered via an impressive 12,500 training days across the country. The training
allows officers to effectively talk down an escalating or potentially dangerous situation.
I expect that this will result in fewer officers being hurt in the line of duty. I have been
told that the training has already led to many tense situations being resolved without the
prisoner involved resorting to violence.

items.speaker: Sandra Goudie
items.text: What other steps have been taken to protect front-line corrections
staff?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Prison staff have already been provided with new
protective equipment for use in dangerous situations. This includes stab-proof vests, spit
hoods, and batons. The department is now starting a 12-month trial of pepper spray,
with a view to adding this tool to the range of safety equipment available to front-line
staff. I am also delighted that our Government is introducing legislation to make
offending against a Department of Corrections officer or a police officer an aggravating
factor in sentencing.
27 Oct 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 14849
Government Accounts, Cash Deficit—Tax Cuts
7. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Labour—New Lynn) to the Minister of Finance:
Why did he continue with his 2010 tax cuts when the Government has a cash deficit of
$9 billion?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Because the package of tax cuts will
lift New Zealand’s rate of growth by improving the incentives to work, to save, to
invest, and to export, and to help a much-needed rebalancing of this economy. The tax
changes have little bearing on the Government’s cash deficit, as they are broadly
fiscally neutral, and are revenue-positive by the end of the forecast period and in future
years. Of course, they will leave the vast majority of New Zealanders a bit better off.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Can he confirm why his old-fashioned recipe of borrow and hope
is going to generate jobs and lead to the creation of new firms, in the face of tax revenue
declining and the Government borrowing over a billion dollars a month, as he
confirmed this morning at the Finance and Expenditure Committee?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I cannot confirm any of that, because it is all wrong. It is
a bit rich being lectured by Labour on borrow and hope. It is a bit like being lectured by
a gambling addict on going to the pokies.

items.speaker: Craig Foss
items.text: Did the Government at any stage borrow in order to give tax cuts?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The answer to that, of course, is no. The income tax cuts of
April 2009 were fully funded by the accompanying changes to KiwiSaver and the
research and development tax credit. The 2010 income tax cuts are funded by an
increase in GST, and by a tightening of the tax regime on foreign investors, smokers,
and people who own investment property. Once this policy is fully in place, it will
produce an annual revenue gain of $175 million a year in 2013, 2014, and beyond then.
Our tax cuts have been good for economic growth and fair for New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I seek leave to table a copy of Budget 2010, showing—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is a shame that the Minister of Finance interjected then; otherwise
Mr Cunliffe might have been taking an early shower. When I get to my feet, he will sit
immediately. The member knows that we do not table copies of the Budget or waste
time during question time on that sort of thing.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Given that he admitted to the Finance and Expenditure Committee
today that his tax cuts were not stimulatory, can he explain to the House why, according
to Budget 2010 documents, he is borrowing ever-increasing amounts of money to pay
for them?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, the member is wrong. The Budget documents do not
show that.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Oh yes, they do.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, no, they do not show that. They show that over 4 years
they are broadly fiscally neutral, and that beyond year 4 there is actually a gain of about
$175 million a year. I do not know which Budget the member is reading.

items.speaker: Craig Foss
items.text: What impact did the 2010 tax package have on income distribution?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As demonstrated in Budget 2010 and the background
documents, the Government spent some time focusing on the distributional impacts of
the tax package. It shows that the gain to the lowest one-third of households by income
was about the same as the gain to the highest one-third of earners. Both groups had their
real after-tax incomes lifted by 0.7 percent. If Labour really thought the tax cuts were
unfair, it would campaign to repeal them. Of course, they are not.
14850 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Oct 2010

items.speaker: Brendon Burns
items.text: Can the Minister tell New Zealand’s hard-working families why
they are paying more GST on everything they buy, when he gets $200 a week in tax
cuts and is borrowing nearly $300 million a week to pay for such cuts?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is not borrowing anything for tax cuts; it
has been a broadly fiscally neutral package. In fact, the Opposition has been
complaining that we put GST up in order to pay for the tax cuts, so it cannot have it
both ways. These are fair tax cuts, but, more important, they help to rebalance this
economy after a decade of mismanagement in which New Zealanders were misled into
believing that borrowing, spending, and speculating on houses were the path to wealth,
when they are not.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given that he admitted to the Finance and Expenditure
Committee today that it cost $450 million in year 1 and $1.045 billion over 4 years to
fund his tax cuts, and that the reason he continued with the tax cuts in April 2009, which
he knew the country could not afford, was that it was a National Party election promise,
why did he raise GST when his Government had promised not to?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: All the member’s assertions are wrong. As I explained to the
member, the tax cuts in April 2009 were actually offset by the changes in KiwiSaver
and the research and development tax credit, which the Opposition often refers to, and
the tax cuts in April 2010 were fiscally neutral. We are very proud that we have
implemented tax cuts that favour saving, exporting, investing, and creating jobs,
whereas the Labour Party favours consumption, borrowing, and excessive Government
spending.
Regulatory Reform—Protection from Compliance Cost Increases
8. Dr CAM CALDER (National) to the Minister for the Environment: What
actions has the Government taken to avoid unnecessary cost increases for New Zealand
householders from excessive regulation?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Regulations passed by the
previous Government would from 1 January prohibit the sale of over 1,000 common
household products sold in cardboard or refill packs, even though the toxicity of those is
little more than table salt or lemon juice. These excessive regulations would have added
over $20 million to family grocery bills and over 30 million plastic containers to the
waste stream. This Government campaigned on removing such unnecessary red tape,
and today it has repealed them.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What products would have been banned from sale, and does any
other country require such regulation for similar household products?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Products that would have been banned from our
supermarket shelves include Surf and Persil. Spray n’ Wipe would not be allowed on
our supermarket shelves, let alone the deadly Palmolive dishwashing liquid. We also
would have had to get rid of—oh, here is the man who is responsible.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I can remember some
time, it might have been last year, but certainly during your reign on the throne, you
prevented the Greens—I think Sue Kedgley—from doing exactly this by using props.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Speaker is considering a genuine point of order. I certainly did
not allow a member to table such things and I did not allow other members to produce
such things, other than the speaking member. But I do not recollect having ruled that a
member with the call could not use props to support what he or she was saying. If I
have, I will apologise for that. I will check back on my record to avoid inconsistency,
and I apologise if I got that wrong. The member has answered considerably; he should
not go on much further.
27 Oct 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 14851

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I think it is very appropriate. The other product that has
been banned is the good old Toilet Duck. These regulations exist in no other developed
country, and are particularly significant for relations with Australia, in that prohibiting
these products makes New Zealand uncompetitive with Australia.

items.speaker: Hon Rodney Hide
items.text: How has the ACT Party and the regulatory reform work led by
me helped identify and reverse these nanny State regulations inherited from the previous
Labour Government?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The Minister who asked the question has initiated a
comprehensive programme of regulatory reform, and when the Grocery Marketers
Association raised these issues with the Minister of Regulatory Reform he insisted on a
review. That review found that these regulations were totally unnecessary and were the
sorts of nanny State regulations that caused the previous Government to be thrown out.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Has the Government reversed all the regulations designed to better
protect children against harmful substances?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No. There are some stronger cleaning products like some
bleaches and concentrated dishwashing powders that do pose a threat that justifies
child-resistant packaging, such as Janola. I hear members opposite arguing that that is
somehow nanny State. I will tell members the difference. The difference is that we are
practical on this side of the House. We apply some common sense rather than banning
these assorted products that would not have been allowed on New Zealand supermarket
shelves if Labour had stayed in Government.

items.speaker: Hon Rodney Hide
items.text: Has the Minister received any advice on the job impacts of these
regulations, given that we would be the only country in the world requiring child-
resistant packaging for products like Surf and Persil?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Yes, I have. It would put New Zealand out on a limb and at
serious disadvantage. I am advised that the Unilever factory in Petone would be put out
of business by these regulations, including the 330 staff who are in the previous
Minister for the Environment’s own electorate. This is a classic example of poor
regulations costing New Zealand householders and costing jobs, and it is one of the
reasons why this Government has a comprehensive programme of regulatory reform.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Before I call the honourable member for the next question, I ask the
Minister to please remove the props, now that he has completed that answer.
Climate Change, Cancun Conference—Legally Binding Agreement
9. Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green) to the Minister responsible for

items.speaker: International Climate Change Negotiations
items.text: Will New Zealand support a legally
binding agreement to cut global greenhouse gas emissions at the Cancun climate change
conference this December; if not, why not?
Hon Dr NICK SMITH (Acting Minister responsible for International Climate
Change Negotiations): Yes, that is this Government’s ambition. This was the position
at Bali, at Copenhagen, and it will also be so at Cancun. However, all indications are
that this is unlikely to be achieved at Cancun, but New Zealand is ready and willing to
make as much progress as is possible.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: If such an agreement is not likely and we are then obliged to
rely on the Copenhagen Accord instead, does he believe that the combined voluntary
emission cuts promised under the Copenhagen Accord will be sufficient to meet the
agreed safe threshold of 2 degrees Celsius, which requires a 28 percent reduction in
global emissions by 2020?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The climate change negotiations are very much the art of
the possible because they require the agreement of over 190 countries on such a
complex issue. It is the Government’s view that the Copenhagen Accord was a second-
14852 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Oct 2010
best outcome from Copenhagen, but it is better than nothing. Our hope is that we will be
able to translate some of the good work that is included in the Copenhagen Accord into
a more robust international agreement.

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: If climate change negotiations are the art of the possible, is it
possible for him to reconcile his plan to cut national emissions by 10 to 20 percent with
a global reduction target of 28 percent, given that as a developed country we are obliged
to take a larger share of the 28 percent, notwithstanding our special situation on
agriculture?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I think it is very important that Parliament understands that
the 10 to 20 percent reduction target range for New Zealand is, of course, based on 1990
emissions, and 1990 emissions grew between then and 2008 by 25 percent, which is a
very substantial increase. The second point that is unique to New Zealand is that, of
course, 50 percent of our emissions come from agriculture, where the technologies are a
lot more challenging. My view is that a 10 to 20 percent reduction from 1990 levels by
2020 is a hugely challenging target for New Zealand.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: What progress has New Zealand made in climate change and will
this enable New Zealand to meet its Kyoto obligations?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: We have made good progress with the emissions trading
scheme coming into effect on 1 July. I am encouraged that the future forecast
projections of emissions show the first years of decline in New Zealand’s net emissions
in any time since 1990—that is, during every year of the previous Labour
administration emissions went up—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: And we had growth and you’ve got a recession!

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The member interjects. It is interesting to note that the big
gains have been firstly in the area of forestry. Under his Government New Zealand
deforested; under our Government we are planting trees. The second big gains have
been in the area of renewable energy, where rather than building thermal power stations,
which occurred under the previous Government, we currently have a record level of
investment in renewable energy, and that should be welcomed.

items.speaker: Hon John Boscawen
items.text: Does he agree with the Greenhouse Policy Coalition that
when comparing New Zealand’s emissions trading scheme with the European Union
emissions trading scheme, from 2015 only 50 percent of emissions in the EU are
covered compared with 100 percent in New Zealand; if so, does he accept that New
Zealand’s emissions trading scheme is more comprehensive than the European
emissions trading scheme and may also render us “uncompetitive with Australia” as the
Minister for the Environment has just explained to the House with reference to his props
of Persil and Surf?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Firstly, in respect of the issue of the comparison with
Australia, it is interesting to note that electricity prices in Australia have gone up by
more than 30 percent over the last 5 years in response to a whole lot of regulatory
measures that Australian Governments have tried—in an inefficient way, in my view—
in order to deal with the challenge of climate change. So I think we are well placed, in
competitive terms, with Australia. In respect of the comparison with Europe, it is very
important that we compare like with like. If we compare our emissions trading scheme
today with that of the European Union, we see that our scheme covers less and is less
aggressive, and we will have a review of the scheme next year. The commitment of this
Government is to ensure that New Zealand does its fair share on climate change, not
that we should try to be a world leader, because we have to carefully balance those
economic and environmental responsibilities.
27 Oct 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 14853
Education, National Standards—Schools’ Comprehension of System
10. Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour—Hutt South) to the Minister of

items.speaker: Education
items.text: What evidence does she have as to the level of understanding of the
Government’s national standards system in schools?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: A range of evidence is available to
me as to the level of understanding of national standards. This includes Education
Review Office data, and results from the Ministry of Education’s monitoring and
evaluation programme, as well as anecdotal evidence from schools I have visited and
people I have met.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Are her standards designed to provide detailed information to
inform the quality of teaching on a daily basis?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The national standards are designed to provide signposts—
expectations of what children should have learnt and by when—to ensure that children
make good progress towards the goal of National Certificate of Educational
Achievement (NCEA) level 2.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It was a very specific
question about whether the national standards are designed to provide information that
would help teaching on a daily basis. The fact that they are designed to do something
else might be taken as a no, but I deliberately asked a very direct question in an attempt
to have it addressed.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I hear what the member is saying—it was a very direct question. I
think the Minister should try to answer that. I accept that she almost did in indicating
what the standards are designed for, but the question actually asked whether they were
designed for that specific issue. It was a very direct question; I think it would be helpful
if the Minister were to answer that.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: As I said, the standards are designed as a set of expectations
of what a child should have learnt in reading, writing, and maths, and by when.
Teachers can use those to guide their teaching, as they do currently, and they can also
use those during the teaching year as they assess—using either assessment tools or their
own teacher judgment—the progress that a student is making.

items.speaker: Allan Peachey
items.text: What evidence has the Minister seen of the level of understanding in
the community about national standards?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I have had numerous emails about national standards from
members of the community that show that they understand the standards, including one
from a board chair, who said: “Since we have implemented the national standards, our
school community has been very happy with the new level of reporting, and we have
had overwhelming positive feedback. Please keep up the good work.”, and this one
from a parent: “We are thrilled with the new national standards, and there are thousands
of parents like us who fully support you and think you and the National-led Government
are on the right track.”

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Is it the Minister’s hope or expectation that the quality of
teaching will improve on a daily basis, based on the information teachers get from
national standards?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The national standards are a set of expectations by which
teachers can measure the progress of their students in reading, writing, and maths.
Quality teaching methods will be used to lift achievement and to accelerate progress
where it is needed, but the standards do not provide that quality teaching.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Can a year 5 student achieve a year 6 standard in reading
comprehension?
14854 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Oct 2010

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I do not have the data in front of me. If the member cares to
put that question in writing, I am happy to provide him with an answer.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Was a backward-mapping exercise carried out to ensure that
progress according to the standards leads to level 2 NCEA in year 12?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It is my understanding that the technical experts who
designed the standards, which were based on the existing literacy progressions that were
introduced under Minister Maharey as Minister of Education, and the numeracy project,
which was introduced when the member who asked the question was Minister of
Education, used those and back-mapped from NCEA level 2, but that is just my advice.
I did not design them. We used technical experts to design them.
State Housing—Challenges
11. HEKIA PARATA (National) to the Minister of Housing: What are the current
challenges the Government is facing with social housing?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: One of the challenges is that a State
house is currently the only benefit in New Zealand where once someone is in, that
person’s need is never reassessed. As a result, we have over 5,000 Housing New
Zealand Corporation tenants paying market rents who could afford to rent from the
landlord next door, and all the while 4,000 families are classified on the waiting list as
high priority for a State house. We also, interestingly, have over 2,700 tenants in homes
that are underutilised, with two or three spare bedrooms. A similar number of tenants,
2,700, are in houses that are deemed to be overcrowded, and really need to be
transferred to a larger property.

items.speaker: Hekia Parata
items.text: Is the Minister able to provide any real life examples of those
situations?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I do have in hand a couple of examples. In Henderson, for
example, we have a tenant in a four-bedroom home who originally lived with her
husband, two adult children, and one dependent child. She is now the only tenant, and
she has three spare bedrooms. If that tenant could have been moved into a smaller
property, the house could be a match for a single mother and her seven young children
who have been living in a garage since her marriage broke up. Four bedrooms would
still be a squeeze, but I think that family of eight would have found it better than the
garage they were often put in, under the previous Government.

items.speaker: Hekia Parata
items.text: What cost does underutilisation have for the New Zealand taxpayer?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Firstly, for every home that is underutilised by two or more
bedrooms, there is a family that is living in overcrowded accommodation. Secondly,
many taxpayers do not realise that they pay Housing New Zealand Corporation the
difference between an income-related rent that tenants pay and the market rent for the
property. The larger the property, generally the larger the subsidy. For example, in
Ōtara we have a single tenant who is living in a four-bedroom house and paying a rent
of $47. There are three spare bedrooms, and the tenant is paying $47 in rent. Other
tenants, of course, are languishing on the waiting list while that person with three spare
bedrooms gets a $21,000 subsidy per year.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Does he agree with Housing New Zealand Corporation staff who
say that the biggest impediment to moving people on from their Housing New Zealand
Corporation home, which the staff try to do now, is not that they refuse to move, but
that they have nowhere to move to, and does he stand by his statement that no tenants
will be made to leave their Housing New Zealand Corporation properties if they do not
have anywhere to go?
27 Oct 2010 Questions for Oral Answer 14855

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: The biggest impediment to Housing New Zealand
Corporation staff moving tenants on, and asking them to be moved on, is that the staff
have not been allowed to ask them to move on in the last decade.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Which parts of the country will see a reduction in the number
Housing New Zealand Corporation properties because they are deemed to have an
oversupply of State housing?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: The areas of the country that will see an increase in the
amount of social housing will be the areas that have high needs. The areas of New
Zealand that will see a decrease in the amount of social housing will be the areas of low
needs. It is not exactly rocket science! I suppose we could be like Labour and build
State houses just in Labour seats, but we are the National Government and we would
rather put houses where the needs are.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: He’s just a show off.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Well, I am.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On this occasion, the Minister himself is lucky that the honourable
deputy leader of the Labour Party interjected or he would have been leaving the House,
because when I get to my feet, even Ministers will sit down. The Minister had said quite
enough, and the question did not justify the last part of that answer. The important thing
is that when I get to my feet, Ministers will sit down. He is just darn lucky that there
was an interjection from the other side of the House or he would be leaving the House. I
insist that that rule will be obeyed.
Pasifika Language Resources—Decision to Stop Publishing Tupu Series and
Folauga
12. SU’A WILLIAM SIO (Labour—Māngere) to the Minister of Education:
Does she stand by her ministry’s decision to stop publishing the five Pacific language
resource Tupu series and the Samoan language Folauga journals that are used by 33
Pacific bilingual units to provide bilingual education to about 1,300 primary students
throughout New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The Ministry of Education has not
decided to stop publishing the Tupu and Folauga series. However, it is reviewing
whether these are the most effective resources to support Pasifika education. This is in
light of the fact that Pasifika students’ literacy levels are consistently and significantly
lower than those for other groups. Schools will continue to receive new titles from the
Tupu and Folauga series in 2010. In addition, a new series of Pasifika language
learning story books have been developed to support the five Pasifika languages
curriculum. These will be distributed to schools starting in November and going through
Su’a William Sio: What evidence does the Minister rely on, when in her own words
“It has been decided to pause Tupu as it does not align with the ministry priority
outcomes of every child achieving literacy and numeracy levels that enable their
success.”?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: As I said in answer to the primary question, in fact the
evidence that the ministry is relying on to review these series is the fact that Pasifika
students’ literacy levels are consistently and significantly lower than those of other
groups.
Su’a William Sio: If the Minister has rejected research recommendations that New
Zealand use Pacific bilingual education to raise Pacific students’ academic
achievements in schools, how does she intend to meet the related objectives of strong
14856 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Oct 2010
identity, self-confidence, and parental aspirations, or is she not concerned that Pacific
people in New Zealand are on a course to lose their first languages for ever?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I totally reject the assertions made in that question. I say to
that member that the ministry will continue to provide language guidelines, resources,
and professional development for teachers to support the teaching of five Pasifika
languages as part of the action from the Pasifika Education Plan 2009-2012. The
Pasifika languages are an integral part of the learning of languages area of the New
Zealand curriculum. These resources also support the preservation and maintenance of
Pasifika languages. In addition, there are a significant number of Tupu and Folauga
books available online.
Su’a William Sio: I seek leave to table a letter signed by the Minister, dated 7
October, and addressed to Joanne Okesene, in which she states that the Tupu series,
which supports language learning, is to be paused.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Members’ Notices of Motion—Leave to Move

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I seek the leave of the House to move members’ notices of motion No. 1, in
the name of Jo Goodhew, right through to No. 64, in the name of Melissa Lee, without
debate. I do this because lots of them move congratulations from many local members
to Commonwealth Games medal-winners. It would be very nice if the House agreed to
do this without debate.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action to be followed. Is there any
objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I move, That the House take
note of miscellaneous business. As New Zealanders, we like to think that our country is
the best place in the world to bring up children. We call New Zealand God’s own. We
say things like: “The future of New Zealand is with our children.”, “Our children are
our greatest assets.”, “Every child deserves a decent standard of living.”, “Every child
should have the ability to reach their full potential.”, and “We value our children, and
children matter.” How many times have we heard those words spoken in this House? I
believe that all those statements are true, and I doubt that any member in the House does
not believe they are true. But are they true for every child in this country? That is the
question that we should be asking ourselves in this House.
Today we heard the compassionate and soft face of National! We heard Judith
Collins answer a question about child poverty and she made it very clear National has
no interest in what happens to children in this country. She has no interest in working
across this House, in line with the request of Every Child Counts that parties in this
House work together for the good of children. The organisation made that request in all
sincerity to this House. Whom does Every Child Counts represent? It represents the
major organisations in New Zealand that look after, and care for, children and families,
from Barnardos and Plunket to kindergartens, iwi organisations, whānau organisations,
and so on.
Every Child Counts is a major organisation, and it has pleaded with this House for us
to form a cross-party group to work for the benefit of children. In good faith I took its
27 Oct 2010 General Debate 14857
request to the Prime Minister of this country, 1 year ago. He turned it down. I have that
letter here and I will seek leave to table it later on. He turned it down and said he was
not interested. He was not interested, and I have waited 1 year to see what this
Government would do in terms of children in this country. I waited to see whether it
would put children first and whether children would become a major focus of this
Government’s expenditure and policy development.
Have we heard about children? As the Child Poverty Action Group said, children
have become invisible in New Zealand. They are invisible to this Government. The
Government will say it has done so much for children. It had an advertising campaign to
stop parents from shaking babies. It has done so much for children that it finds it hard to
write it on a postage stamp!
Well, the truth is New Zealand is not doing well for our children; we are not doing as
well as comparable countries. We sit at the bottom third of the OECD rankings in terms
of most child indicators. Many of our children in this country are left behind. Their
early life experiences are harmful and ongoing. Many Māori and Pasifika children have
poorer life chances than other children of the same age.
Contrary to Mrs Collins’ statements in this House, the Labour Government did make
some progress on child poverty in this country. We made it with positive actions like
Working for Families, which took 132,000 families out of poverty in this country. We
brought in affordable primary health care to reduce the cost of going to the doctor. We
restored income-related rents and introduced 20 free hours of early childhood education.
And we reduced the number on the unemployment benefit to 22,000, compared with the
65,000 we have now, and that number is growing.
But I have to say that is not enough. As far as Labour is concerned, there is
unfinished business when it comes to child poverty in this country. We ask the
Government whether it will do something about it. It has had 2 years to address child
poverty. We heard today that it will not make a commitment to reducing child poverty
in this country. I need to tell those members opposite who sit on the front bench and
make out that they care about children that child poverty in this country is growing yet
again. The numbers are going up right now and they will continue to go up, as long as
the Government continues to follow its current policies. I recently read Plunket’s annual
report in which it stated: “You need to invest in the first 3 years of life.”

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: My challenge for the
deputy leader of the Labour Party is to explain how petty regulations, passed by her
Government, would help child poverty. How would banning products like Cuddly
somehow help the children of New Zealand? The real issues facing our country are how
we make living more affordable for families and how we secure jobs for New Zealand. I
say to members opposite that one of the positive things we can do is to repeal some of
the stupid regulations that were passed by the previous Labour Government. I knew that
Labour had passed laws to ban types of light bulbs. I knew it had passed regulations to
tell New Zealanders what size showerheads they were allowed to use. I knew it had
passed laws that said people could not do DIY work on their own houses. Never in my
wildest dreams did I expect that products like Surf, Persil, and Mr Muscle—to mention
Rodney Hide; or Toilet Duck, to represent Mr Mallard; or Cuddly, to represent Parekura
Horomia—would be banned. Never in my wildest dreams did I think Labour would be
so stupid as to ban those sorts of products.
Members are chuckling. Let me just remind them of the real impact of those sorts of
stupid policies. I am advised that that regulation would add $20 million a year—$20
million a year—to household grocery bills. How dare members opposite get up in this
House and shed crocodile tears about the cost of living when they passed such silly
regulations. It is even more serious than that. You see, the sort of regulation that would
14858 General Debate 27 Oct 2010
add those sorts of costs would put hundreds of New Zealanders out of work. No other
country in the world has those regulations. How is the Unilever plant in Lower Hutt,
which produces products like Surf and Persil, able to be internationally competitive with
the sorts of stupid regulations that members opposite put into our law books? I ask
Trevor Mallard, who is defending those rules, why he cares so little about those 330
jobs.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Drink it, Smith.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I think that interjection states the difference between
members of the Government and members of the Opposition. They somehow believe in
their nanny State minds that we have to regulate absolutely every element of life to
protect children. I have checked with the poison centre and I have checked with
Safekids, the advocacy group—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Drink it now.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The pathetic interjection from Mr Mallard is for me to
drink it. Is he saying that every single product on the supermarket shelves that might
cause people harm has to have some special child-resistant packaging? That is what he
is saying and that is what he put in the law books.
I say that common-sense New Zealanders know that that is a nonsense. They know
that they do not do it in Australia. They know that they do not do it in the US. They
know that they do not do it in the European Union. It is a classic example of the petty,
nanny State regulations that drive New Zealanders mad. Nor does it make any
environmental sense at all, as 30 million extra plastic bottles would go into the system
each year—30 million extra plastic bottles—if we followed the regulations that Mr
Mallard sat over. It is the issue that separates the common sense on this side of the
House with the nanny State regulators who would push up the costs and who would put
New Zealanders out of work while they run this country mad with red tape. Thankfully,
this Government has the common sense to deregulate that sort of nonsense and apply a
little common sense to the business of Government.

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.
I did not rise to my feet during the middle of that speech out of courtesy to the Minister,
but throughout that speech and especially towards the end of it the former Minister
across the House, the Hon Trevor Mallard, was shouting out repeatedly: “Liar, liar,
liar.” It is unacceptable in this House, and I expect the Hon Trevor Mallard to withdraw
and apologise.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Speaking to the point of order—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not think that I need to hear further on the matter. In fact, he
was not interjecting that. I was listening very carefully. I was not so happy with his
interjections, but he was disputing what the Minister was saying. He definitely did not
call the Minister a liar; he did not use the word “liar”. I listened very carefully to the
interjections. But it is not helpful to the good order of the House to use that kind of
language when interjecting. Neither is it to the good order of the House to use a
member’s last name, which the member was also interjecting further with. I ask
members to be a bit more reasonable. Had the member interjected what Chris Tremain
suggested, then I would definitely ask the member to withdraw and apologise, but he
did not actually say that.

items.speaker: Hon RODNEY HIDE
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You
are right in part, but at the end of that speech Trevor Mallard called out: “He’s a liar.”
When Chris Tremain was making his point, Annette King nodded her head. I certainly
heard Trevor Mallard say that the Minister is a liar. I think you should ask Trevor
Mallard whether that is what he said.
27 Oct 2010 General Debate 14859

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If members have taken objection, I will ask the honourable member.
I did not hear him say that. I heard him say “It’s a lie, what the Minister is saying.”, but
I did not hear him call the Minister a liar. I say to the honourable member—

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I did.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I ask—

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No, before you do, I say that the Standing Orders are
very clear that members are required to take points of order on these matters at the time
they occur, and no member did.

items.speaker: Hon Rodney Hide
items.text: Speaking to the point of order—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I do not need further help on this. Members do not want to
disrupt speeches, but that is no excuse. If the member actually called the Minister a
liar—I did not hear it—I ask the member to withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the honourable member.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I seek leave to table a
letter from the New Zealand Food and Grocery Council to me and the Minister for
Regulatory Reform, Rodney Hide, dated 15 February, entitled “Regulatory tsunami
warning”.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Before I call the next speaker, I apologise to the honourable
member Chris Tremain for my not having heard the matter he objected to and doubting
his point of order. I apologise to him.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I rise to address the issue of climate change
and this Government’s failure to develop adequate national policy to combat it.
Climate change has slipped below the threshold of daily media focus, and that is the
way that this Government seems to want it. The failure at Copenhagen to tackle the
global threat head on has sent the international community into a state of collective
catatonia. We see this in the lack of leadership from the UN, in the actions of national
Governments around the world, and in the attitude of much of the public around the
world.
The problem we have is that nature is not disposed to wait for humanity to iron itself
out morally and get its political act together. The poor countries rail against us for
historical responsibility and insufficient reduction targets. The rich countries fear the
projected population growth among the poor and insist that they enter binding
commitments before we sign on to medium-term cuts.

items.speaker: Humanity probably faces only two global threats
items.text: immolation through nuclear
conflict, or suffocation through global warming. The first is the product of traditional
enmity; the enemy was the other tribe or the other nation. Climate change is the product
of a new enemy: us. We try to cut nuclear arsenals by changing the enemy’s behaviour;
we are required to cut carbon emissions by changing our own behaviour. It is no
surprise that we are not succeeding. Most Governments lack the political courage to
convey the magnitude of the climate change threat to their peoples, and they lack the
political insight to prescribe the required global and national policies that are necessary.
Before, during, and since Copenhagen the threat of serious unpredictable climate
change has grown. Our scientists do not know when non-linear change might occur, but
they warn that tipping points exist. If the precautionary principle is to mean anything,
we must all move with speedy purpose and resolve. Translated politically, that means
we must act not as an international community of States, but as a global community of
14860 General Debate 27 Oct 2010
peoples who are represented by Governments. If the difference seems vanishingly
small, then we do well to act on it none the less, lest our prospects of survival prove to
be the same.
Our professional negotiators are rearranging the deckchairs contemplating whether
we shall have one or two legal agreements, and whether it will be next year, or 3 or 10
years from now. Our political leaders dampen our expectations with appeals to realism.
We all suffer from cognitive dissonance. Every so often we see the magnitude and
imminence of the threat, but it is simply too frightening to accept individually and
politically, so we basically return to business and government as usual.
As the Minister made clear recently in question time, the state of play is the
Copenhagen Accord, with voluntary commitments to national cuts. These are
demonstrably inadequate to the science-based judgment of what is required to avert
failure, but we pretend that it is a useful start to greater things. We are told that global
emissions must peak within about 7 years, and we know that the accord is way, way
short of achieving that, so we mumble about bigger cuts later and avoid looking into our
children’s eyes.
Let us address some facts. To achieve a 2 degrees Celsius threshold, we must reduce
our global carbon budget from 50 gigatonnes today to 36 by 2020, and to seven by
2050. The rich countries must cut from about 40 today to 11 by 2020 and to one by
2050. That is correct: we in the rich world must emit only one gigatonne in 2050, out of
the seven emitted by the world that year. It is called contraction and convergence, and it
is the only way humanity will successfully deal with climate change. That is when our
moral and political standards merge at the global level. After 10 millennia, especially
the past two centuries, it is the moment of truth.
For our part, New Zealand has to agree through treaty or by voluntary declaration in
advance to cut our national emissions proportionately. That means we must cut from 78
million tonnes today to 56 million tonnes in 2020, down to 1.6 million in 2050. That is
the scale of the challenge before New Zealand. It is as well that we face up to it now,
not when it is too late.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I appreciate this opportunity to
address the House. It would be fair to say that the National Government team, the MP
team and certainly the team in Cabinet, are very, very positive about the progress that
we have made in the last 2 years, while going through a very, very difficult time. In the
area of my portfolio I could not be happier with the way that Housing New Zealand
Corporation has managed its work during this recession. There has been more pressure
on the State house waiting list and on the stock than we have seen for a couple of
decades. Why? Because during the worldwide recession many, many families have
come under pressure, either because of the loss of jobs or because of reduced hours
being worked. Because of the difficulties in a worldwide recession, families have had to
close their cheque books, and their ability to spend on simple items such as rent,
mortgages, and those types of things has become quite difficult. During that time
Housing New Zealand Corporation has managed to maintain the waiting list at a level
that has been typical of the last decade. We have not seen the waiting list shoot up by
3,000 or anything like that; it has tended to oscillate at around the 10,000 mark.
I have to commend the corporation, because it has done this through a variety of
means. One, of course, is the Options and Advice Service, which the National
Government introduced. When people rock up to Housing New Zealand Corporation
and say they need a State home, instead of the corporation writing down their names
and putting them on the waiting list it now takes them through some options. One
option is to remain where they are. The corporation asks whether it can help them to
remain where they are, and outlines subsidies like the accommodation supplement.
27 Oct 2010 General Debate 14861
Another option is private rental—the possibility that they could rent privately. The
corporation outlines subsidies for them to do that.
Another option, of course, is homeownership. Here is a good one; this will fascinate
members. In the last 18 months about 400 people have walked into Housing New
Zealand Corporation—so that members do not misunderstand this, I say thousands of
people have walked into Housing New Zealand Corporation, but they have included 400
people in particular who would, under the previous Labour Government, have been put
on the waiting list. Can members guess what those people did after talking to the
Options and Advice Service? Members will not believe this: they went to buy a home.
The previous Government would have put them on the waiting list. They got some
advice, turned round on their heels, went out, and it was their intention to buy a home.
The Labour Government would have put them on the waiting list. It is unbelievable. All
that Housing New Zealand Corporation did was to ask them whether they were sure that
they wanted to go on the waiting list. Those people asked whether there were other
options, and the corporation said yes, there were options like staying where they were,
and the corporation would help them; renting privately; renting with another community
housing provider; or even buying a home. They said: “Oh, we could buy a home?”. We
said that if they wanted to do that, we could even help them to do so.
The previous Labour Government would have told those people to go on the waiting
list. They loved it for people like them to become welfare beneficiaries, because then
they would become dependent on the great Labour Party and vote for it for the rest of
their lives. Well, here is a crack-up: 400 people turned on their heels and decided that
rather than going into a State house, they preferred to go and buy a home. Many of
them, I understand, have pursued that.
For the very same reason we believe that it is worthwhile to look at the almost
70,000 houses that we now have under the corporation’s management, and to ask
whether we are always housing the people who are most in need—because the answer is
no. The reality is that when we have a couple in Māngere at this very moment who have
a four-bedroom home, and who originally had one adult child and two dependent
children—so that is five people in a four-bedroom house—but who now live alone with
three spare bedrooms, those tenants could be matched to a one or two-bedroom home.
We have another single mother with three children boarding with relatives in a garage in
Māngere, and they should be in the home that has three spare bedrooms. That is why we
are not ashamed to make this conversation public and have a debate on the issue.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: It is evident that the
Government is starting to worry, because time after time in the House today every
question was about what Labour is doing. Time after time in the House today every
member on the Government side talked only about what Labour has done or is doing,
not about what they are doing. They are worried about the messages that are not
resonating out there with the public.
We can take Nick Smith, for example; his whole contribution was just about child-
resistant caps on bottles. We cannot buy Listerine today without a child-resistant cap;
we cannot buy Janola today without a child-resistant cap. It is not about packaging, per
se; it is about ensuring that our kids are safe from some of the harshest household
substances in our homes. Usually, those substances are in the bottom cupboard under
the sink by the washing machine, or under the kitchen sink. Labour wanted to ensure
that everyday families could keep their kids safe by having child-resistant caps on those
substances. Anything more than that is pure fabrication by the Minister for the
Environment, and should be left as that.
We know that when we put children at the centre of our thinking, it is about making
the types of changes that can make a real difference in everyday homes to Kiwis around
14862 General Debate 27 Oct 2010
New Zealand. We know that New Zealanders are excited about the message that our
deputy leader gave to the annual conference. She said that we will unreservedly ensure
that children are at the centre of our policy framework. More important, children will be
at the centre of the actions that we will take in moving forward if we should be elected
in the 2012 election.
We build on a foundation that has really supported children: affordable general
practitioner visits, free health care for under-sixes, and affordable health care visits
where, when mum takes baby to the doctor, she pays $10 or nothing for her child. That
is set to change under National, and families are worried about that. We know that
families who are on fixed and low incomes have actually had a better deal under Labour
with income-related rentals, but that is set to change under National. Working for
Families has helped low and modest income families who are partly working and want
to get ahead. That scheme has helped but is probably set to be changed under National.
The 20 free hours’ early childhood education policy was brought in by Labour, and that
is set to change under National—but there will be more about that later.
Most important, certainly for the families that I represent, during the time that
Labour was in Government Māori unemployment dropped from 19 percent to 6 percent.
We believe in work for families. Jobs were there, and our families were working. But I
ask Minister Collins where the jobs are now. She got up in the House today and said the
best type of support for families is work, but where are the jobs? She could not answer
that question. Minister Heatley got up in the House and said all those things that are
happening in State houses, but we know that out in our communities there are not
enough State houses in some areas. In Thames, for example, they tell us that there are
not enough State houses, and families there have to go on to market-related rentals. The
average cost of a three-bedroom home is $280 to $320 a week, and those houses have a
holiday clause. Those families have to get out in December, and they can possibly go
back in about February, because those private landlords will get more from renting out
their homes in that way, so they will just let the tenants go. They do not care whether
those tenants have a home.
Key things are happening out in our communities under this Government that will
put children at risk. But we know that we have to invest in the early years. We
understand that more and more Kiwi families are making the decision to come home
and bring up their children, because they want to bring up their children in New
Zealand, but they are not supported by the current changes that this type of Government
is making.
I visited He Taonga te Mokopuna, which is a teen parent unit. Labour was very
proud of supporting young people who found themselves pregnant at a young age, and
who wanted to continue in education. We knew that supporting them to continue their
education would make a real difference. We introduced a young parent allowance that
would help them, helping their children to be at a childcare centre while the young
parents learnt. We are starting to see young parents actually graduate from tertiary
education with the support of the types of policies that Labour brought in. But all of that
is set to change under National, and those members are harping on about things that
make very little difference.

items.speaker: Hon PANSY WONG
items.text: I think that that member
Nanaia Mahuta has forgotten, with all of those policies that she talked about, that
Labour was thrown out of office in 2008, so I do not know where the fresh thinking is
coming from.
The National-led Government has so many initiatives to talk about that I am spoilt
for choice. I thought that I would pick one that is really exciting: I welcome members to
128C Preston Road, Ōtara; the most stunning three-bedroom, first-home buyers’ dream
27 Oct 2010 General Debate 14863
home. I wish that when I was looking for my first home this stunning three-bedroom
home had been available. Last Friday it was such a pleasure for me, Dr Cam Calder, and
Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi to support two of our hard-working, innovative Ministers, the
Hon Maurice Williamson and the Hon Phil Heatley.
Under this National-led Government, we do not impose things in passing laws. Dr
Nick Smith demonstrated the ridiculousness of rules that were always imposed by
Labour. Labour always thinks that it knows best for New Zealanders; that is why it was
turfed out in 2008. For a difference, look at this stunning sitting room in this three-
bedroom home, which cost only $168,000 to build. That was the result of the National-
led Government’s initiative called the Simple House Acceptable Solution.
The Department of Building and Housing put the initiative together to ensure that
people who want to build their first home can look at the requirements, get the
instructions about structural strength and durability, and know what should be done to
satisfy those requirements, for a finish that will reflect the requirement for durability
and flexibility to meet changes. All those requirements are contained in this first-home
package. Guess what? The best thing is that for a very long time people complained
about waiting for months, if not years, for building consents, but this initiative reduces
the consent process to days. We are talking about days, not weeks.
The day when we were at the house, we were standing at the beautiful courtyard and
looking into that three-bedroom home, which is now so affordable for the first-home
buyer. It can be built by anybody, anywhere in New Zealand. It can be built on any
land, in any style. All they have to do is satisfy this very simple initiative, called the
Simple House Acceptable Solution. That is the style of National. We want to make
homes that can be built faster and be more affordable. More than that, we want to make
homes that are stunning and that have flexibility. Future so-called cheap housing is
actually a dream for anybody. This house alone—I am sure Dr Cam Calder, who was
there with me last Friday, would agree—will transform people’s images of cheap
housing.
I think that lots of people now will rush in. Wait until next summer, when this house
will be up for auction. Some very lucky couple will be able to say: “Wow, that’s the
type of Government that I can support, because it turns young people’s dream homes
into a reality.” Anybody would be proud to own this home, to bring up their children
