and enjoy barbecues, which are coming up in summertime. Think about what this is
doing to the Ōtara suburb. I am so proud of Ōtara and Manukau because this is the type
of contemporary thinking they need.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: That was the Minister of Women’s Affairs, who did
not once mention this Government’s track record on women’s affairs. Is it any wonder?
The Government has gone backwards so fast on women’s issues that she could not even
clock it. The way a Government spends its money shows its priorities, even in
recessionary times. That is why it is shameful that the largest cut has been to early
childhood education. That cut shows that the Government does not care about this
nation’s children. It showed us as much when Nick Smith, at question time, gloated
about taking away child-resistant caps so that young children may not be safe. They will
be able to get into the laundry detergent in the wash houses of the very houses that
Pansy Wong just spoke about.
The public is starting to ask what this Government has against children. They have
noticed that when the funding cuts came, they hit the very youngest, most vulnerable
children in our community, who are those aged under 5. It was the cuts to early
childhood education that showed what a low priority children are to this National
Government. That is despite what all the research says. All the research tells us that it is
early childhood education, in the years from birth to 6 that really makes the difference
14864 General Debate 27 Oct 2010
to life outcomes from there on in. That is where the investment should go. Even the
Prime Minister’s own science adviser, Sir Peter Gluckman, told the Prime Minister this.
That is where the investment should go, but the Prime Minister has allowed funding
cuts to early childhood education in the years from birth to 6 years of age. That shows a
lack of priority for children.
Then the Government set up a task force. After making funding cuts, the Minister
decided to overhaul the whole early childhood education sector. I can tell members that
I have just been to a conference this very morning, here in Wellington, and the early
childhood education sector is up in arms. It was not consulted at all about the review, it
had no say over the membership of the review, and it is very concerned that there does
not appear to be anyone on the review panel who has any experience of working in early
childhood education, at all. It is chaired by one Michael Mintrom. I am very worried
about what I read about Mr Mintrom. He does not come from the early childhood
education sector so we do not know a great deal about him. In the year 2000 he wrote a
book called Policy Entrepreneurs and School Choice. The premise of that book is
“Understanding how policy ideas catch on, even when their workability remains in
doubt.” What does that tell us about where this task force is headed? “Understanding
how policy ideas catch on, even when their workability remains in doubt.”, is the type
of comment that causes the sector grave concern over what this task force may well
come out with. It represents yet another broken promise from National.
I do not know whether members opposite have recently dug out the National Party’s
policy on early childhood education at the last election. Almost every promise in that
document has been broken already. The first thing National promised was that it would
enhance 20 hours’ early childhood education by keeping the existing subsidies and fee
controls. Yet Anne Tolley told us just yesterday that she has scrapped two of the
subsidies that supported 20 hours’ free early childhood education. She admitted that
yesterday in Parliament. That promise has been broken. Then National went on to say
that it would reduce staff ratios. That is what it promised going into the last election, but
because of Anne Tolley’s and John Key’s funding cuts to early childhood education,
staff are being sacked from that sector. That means that children are in environments
that have fewer adults and fewer staff who are involved in early childhood education.
That reduces quality and reduces staff ratios. It is yet another National Party broken
election promise on early childhood education.
Families are feeling very betrayed. They believed National when it said that it would
leave early childhood education alone. It clearly has not done that. National has broken
its promises to those families because it does not prioritise children. I was shocked,
because another broken promise from National—and I was in the room—was when
Every Child Counts asked for a cross-parliamentary group to support children.

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Huri noa i tō tātou Whare. I
am delighted to stand and speak about how the National-led Government’s aspirational
programme is having effect and being embraced by the good people of the Mana
electorate. I am determined to bring an even stronger voice for the Mana electorate in
the John Key Government, and I am absolutely determined to sound out the full story of
the Mana electorate.
We have had access to Ministers, which is one of the features of being in
Government. I have been able to have Dr Nick Smith, for instance, visit the Mana
electorate and celebrate the memorandum of understanding that has been drawn up by
the Porirua City Council, the Greater Wellington Regional Council, and 12 other
agencies, all of whom are committed to restoring the water quality of the Porirua
Harbour and the Pāuatahanui inlet. This work anticipates the report of the Land and
27 Oct 2010 General Debate 14865
Water Forum, and Dr Smith was absolutely delighted to see the forward-thinking
leadership of the people who are in local government in the Mana electorate.
The Minister of Housing, the Hon Phil Heatley, has visited Mana. It was an
opportunity for him to see and focus on the work and challenges that lie ahead of us
because of the considerable deferred maintenance from the time of the previous
Government, and it shows the importance that we have placed on, for instance, the
makeover of Hampshire Street in Porirua East and the refurbishment of Flora Street.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Has the member ever been there?

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: The member has indeed been there, more times than that
member has had breakfast. He has seen the Flora Street refurbishment. He has
announced the opening of the Gateway Housing programme, in collaboration with
Habitat for Humanity, on Beauzami Crescent, which is in Waitangirua, I say for that
member’s edification.
Yesterday the Minister of Police, Judith Collins, visited. We took the unprecedented
opportunity of thanking the volunteers in the community police bases, which have
flourished under this National-led Government. We visited the community police base
in Tītahi Bay, we went to Cannons Creek, and we went across to Whitby and down to
Mana. It was a veritable Cook’s tour of the Mana electorate, where every day volunteers
commit some time to looking after their community—reflecting our Government’s
focus and emphasis on community safety—and where police are part of the community.
That was clearly shown to us.
Let me tell members that the Kapiti-Mana policing area has the lowest crime rate in
the Wellington region. This is contrary to the stereotypes that those more negative
commentators wish to perpetuate, so much so that I will just tell the House a true story.
A community constable was late getting to the meeting yesterday afternoon, because in
the course of his duties he had been chasing an escaped criminal. Having caught the
criminal and taken him down the Porirua police station, he found that the criminal had a
record of over 160 convictions. The constable asked him what he was doing there,
because he was not a usual resident of the Porirua area. His reply, which was absolutely
reflective of the Porirua area, was: “I have moved to Porirua because it is safer.” That
was from a felon with a conviction sheet of over 160 convictions. He moved to Porirua
because it is safer there.
During the course of the past few weeks, I also had the opportunity to have the Prime
Minister visit, from Raumati in the north—for those members who are not familiar with
the Mana electorate—to Linden in the south. Throughout the course of these visits he
had people coming up to him, saying what a wonderful economic management
programme this Government has in place, whether it is Lembas Café in Raumati South,
which won a Wellington on a Plate title, or whether—[Interruption] Members opposite
may wish to deride this, but I am speaking about real people, rather than about the
theory of invective that usually flows from the other side of the House. Whether it is
Trudy at the wonderful Cafe Vella in Plimmerton, or Belinda at the equally fabulous
Peppermill Delicatessen in central Porirua, all of these women in business—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: The people in Cannons Creek go to cafes all the time, don’t
they?

items.speaker: HEKIA PARATA
items.text: —are backing themselves, I say to Mr Lees-Galloway, because
they are enthused and encouraged by this Government’s programme.
SU’A WILLIAM SIO (Labour—Māngere): I had the opportunity on Sunday to
visit some friends and relatives, and to talk with Kris Fa’afoi and church leaders in
Cannons Creek. I am surprised by what the previous speaker, Hekia Parata, just said,
because after meeting church leaders and families, I can say to this House with much
confidence that many working families there are suffering under this Government.
14866 General Debate 27 Oct 2010
Many families there are suffering under the tax switch; many working families there are
suffering because of the lack of jobs, and the lack of having a plan, at all, by this
Government.
The majority of those who are hurting under this Government and its particular
policies are the children of Mana. It is the desire of every family that I met in Mana on
Sunday to have the best for their children. They want the best opportunities in education
and in health, and I have no doubt that that dream is shared by people up and down this
country—our children are the future leaders of this nation. But I have said to those
families that under this National Government we will have to fight for that dream if we
want it to come true.
The next Labour Government, under Phil Goff and Annette King, will put children at
the centre of policy in health, education, housing, and social development. We have to
put children at the centre of those policies if we are to achieve the dream for our
children and for future generations. But as I said to the people of Mana, with their help
we have to fight for it if we want to achieve it. We will not achieve it under this
Government, so we have to fight for it if we want children to be the centre of our
education policy. We have to fight for it if we want our children to be strong and
healthy in the future. New Zealanders have to fight for it, because under this
Government we will never achieve any of these dreams or aspirations.
The last time the Nats were in Government, in 1990 to 1999 under Jim Bolger and
Jenny Shipley, the period was marked by industrial unrest and by the widening divide of
inequality. The children of that period suffered under the same failed economic right-
wing policies that this Government is now bringing up again. Wages were driven down
and unemployment reached unprecedented highs during that particular period.
Labour in its last term in Government worked extremely hard to ensure that we
regained some of the losses suffered under that National Government. Working for
Families helped to reduce child poverty. We had affordable primary health care so that
our children who had been unhealthy under that previous National Government could
access a doctor and go to the hospital when that was required. Labour restored income-
related rents. Under that National Government, people were kicked out of their homes
and the housing stock was left unsupported. Labour introduced 20-hours’ free early
childhood education and we reduced unemployment. But all the gain that was made in 9
years we have lost in only 2 years under John Key’s National Government. We have
lost it, and the inequality gap continues to widen.
Industrial unrest is what we saw at Labour weekend. Unemployment is increasing,
and the children of our ordinary families up and down the country continue to suffer
under this Government. This is not a family-friendly Government; it is not a child-
friendly Government. Under this Government, failed right-wing economic policies are
widening the gap, so we are losing. Our families, the people of Mana, and the people up
and down this country will have to fight if we are going to regain ground and put
children at the centre of policies.
If we want to achieve the dreams of our children, our future leaders, we will have to
fight to get a Labour Government in office. I know that the people of Mana will bring
Kris Fa’afoi back as their MP, because they will fight for it.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: I heard only a few weeks ago from
one of New Zealand’s leading children’s organisations that the former, failed Labour
Government, under its Working for Families policy, failed thousands of New Zealand
children.
But there is good news. Health is better, sooner, and more convenient. We notched
up yet another success last Friday with the opening of Waiuku Health Plus, a primary
integrated medical health centre, by the Minister of Health and me in the excellent
27 Oct 2010 General Debate 14867
Hunua electorate, which is, by chance, the very electorate that I am privileged to
represent. It is yet another sign of the significant gains to health services under the
National Government. Firstly, I congratulate Dr Mark Eustace, his wife, Jo, the many
medical staff and other colleagues, and the developer. They were prepared to put in their
own personal capital, take risks, and develop one of the finest integrated centres I have
seen anywhere in the world. It will be the lifeline of this rural community for many,
many years to come. The facilities include doctors’ surgeries, specialist facilities,
physiotherapists, pharmacy facilities, even a hypnotherapist, and much, much more.
This is a magnificently designed building that will serve the primary-care needs of that
rural community, and it will be replicated throughout the country over the years to
come.
The point I want to make is that this was done with a sympathetic district health
board in a climate in which the public health system and the Minister of Health
collaborated with the private system, unlike a phenomenon I recall from some years ago
when Helen Clark, the then Labour Prime Minister, refused to turn up to the opening of
the futuristic and excellent Ascot Integrated Hospital, because she said she did not
believe in a private health system. What a dreadful indictment!
It is no coincidence that the Waiuku doctors had wanted to carry out a public-private
partnership on the site of the old Franklin Memorial Hospital 5, 6, or 7 years ago. But at
that time, under the climate of a Labour Government, they were literally obstructed.
There was nothing they could do. Instead, they took the initiative into their own hands.
They were prepared to take the risks and they have built this very forward-looking,
excellent community facility that will serve the community for so long. The National
Government will encourage this exercising of choice for the people of New Zealand.
The recent passage of the New Zealand Public Health and Disability Amendment
Bill was historic in that all submitters agreed to it, as did all parties—even the Labour
Party. This means that New Zealand health services will be not be subject to the
electoral swings that have occurred vastly over the last 20 or 30 years. An insightful
National Government has brought in well-crafted legislation, and that legislation
ensures that we run an efficient, effective health service in which every health dollar
counts, which is something that the former Minister of Health the Hon Annette King
failed to do in the health system, which was reflected by the Labour Government’s
doubling the amount of money spent for no extra services.
The other thing that the New Zealand Public Health and Disability Amendment Bill
will do is ensure that back-office bureaucracy is minimised and the resources moved to
the front line, which is something that will be more and more prevalent under this
excellent National Government.

items.speaker: Hon Sir ROGER DOUGLAS
items.text: For the past 15 years New Zealand has been
slipping slowly—some people would say, not so slowly—into economic difficulty;
some might even say that it is headed towards chaos. This has happened over the past
15 years because both Labour and National have been prepared to compromise any
principles they claim to have. We have seen a preparedness to write a cheque for
whatever demands the latest focus-group puts out there. The worst case of this was
probably at the 2005 election when Labour was re-elected, probably thanks to interest-
free student loans. That did the trick. This year it is putting up the idea that it would take
GST off some items of food. That is why New Zealand is in economic difficulty. I must
say that it is not helped by a National Government that says: “These things are sacred.
We will not touch the interest-free student loans.”, even when it knows it is madness;
“We will not look at the age of retirement of 65.”, when it knows that the big issue that
will confront New Zealand over the next 10 or 20 years is the clash between young and
old, as the young start to say that they are either leaving this country, or they are not
14868 General Debate 27 Oct 2010
prepared to pay for the benefits at the current level. The National Government will not
touch Working for Families and it will not even look at the issue of privatisation, even if
it means higher productivity.
The fact is that we as a nation are borrowing $250 million a week, or $13 billion a
year. For a family of four, we are borrowing about $240 a week. We have had a
situation where over the last 11 years this country has increased Government
expenditure out of all proportion to what is reasonable. We have seen a situation
whereby Government spending per person under Labour increased over 9 years by
$5,500 in real terms, and in 2 years under National it has increased by $1,500 in real
terms. Government spending has increased by $7,000 per person in real terms, or by
$525 a week for a family of four.
We might well ask what we as a nation get for that increased spending of $7,000 per
person, or $525 a week for a family of four. Do all children receive a decent education
as a result of this massive increase in public spending? No. Do most people retire with
enough money to live in comfort in this country? No. Does everyone receive health
treatment when they need it? We have increased public expenditure by $7,000 per
person, or by $525 a week for a family of four. Do they get health treatment when they
need it? No. Have we eradicated poverty? No. On the very goals that the welfare State
has sought to achieve, no one in this country can genuinely argue that we have
succeeded. Even the modern-day proponents of the welfare State, be it National,
Labour, the Greens, or the Māori Party know deep down that it has failed. But they
think they have the solution, that all we need to do is increase spending; but increasing
Government spending by $7,000 per person in real terms over 11 years has not done
it—maybe $10,000 will! The fact is that National and Labour should apologise to the
people of this country. They do not really care. The only thing they care about is re-
election.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: What a privilege it is to be a small part
in the John Key - led National Government. To some extent, I go along with some of
the things that the previous speaker, Sir Roger Douglas, has said, because he is right.
Actually, the National Government does have a $13 billion deficit this year.
We are borrowing $256 million a week, I think, to keep things going and to ensure
entitlements, and does it not just show the lie in Labour politics when those members
come into this House and talk about all the cuts and the cutbacks? We are keeping
things going. We are a centrist Government, which is doing the right things at the right
moments in this country’s economy. [Interruption] Many people say such very rude
things about Trevor Mallard, but I do not mind him. I saw an uncommon act of
humanity when Sir Roger Douglas tipped over his glass of water—Trevor Mallard went
over and did something about it. I like that; that is the sort of thing I expect a National
MP to do, but it was very good of him to do that.
I will talk about the tax cuts, because I have not had the chance in this House since 1
October to talk about them, and now we know that they are bedded in. The remarkable
thing—again, something that shows the lie in Labour politics—is how well the tax cuts
have worked. Despite all the scaremongering by Labour, I am not getting emails any
more from people complaining about GST, because they are seeing the very real impact
the tax cuts are having across the board for them. People are seeing the money in their
pockets. They are feeling it. They are very, very happy about the tax cuts.
I am not an economist; I am the first to admit that. But I know that when we have $2
billion in GST rises and we have $4 billion going out in tax cuts across the board, that
means that 73 percent of Kiwis have a top marginal tax rate of 17.5 percent. That has to
be good, not just for fat cats but for all Kiwis on all incomes. We have done a very good
thing there.
27 Oct 2010 General Debate 14869
In electorates like Tauranga, Ōtaki, and Hutt South, which Trevor Mallard
represents, where there are significant populations of elderly people, the news is best for
them. Over the last couple of years an average married couple on superannuation, with a
home, has had $100 extra. They have had an additional $40 in compensation with the
tax cuts, so they are substantially better off.
One does not need to be an economist to know that there is more cash in people’s
pockets as a result of what National has done. One does not need to be an economist to
know that with inflation at 1.5 percent, things are going pretty well in terms of prices
staying where they are. After-tax wages are much higher than they have been in the last
5 or 6 years, I think, under Labour, and Labour members do not like it. There has been
real after-tax wage growth. It is not miracle stuff.
Slowly but surely we are putting things in place. We are putting the incentives in
place. We have lowered taxes. We are increasing the infrastructure spend, with all the
efficiency that that brings. We are bringing better, smarter public services, moving
things to the front line. We are reforming the regulations. We are bringing in education
and skills in a way that Trevor Mallard, frankly—I know he tried his best—could not
do. We are encouraging business innovation and trade in this country. I repeat what I
said when I started: it really is a privilege to be part of this National-led Government—

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: You said “a small part”.

items.speaker: SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Yes, a small part—small in stature—but, nevertheless, I am
privileged to have a part in this Government, led by John Key, as we do a lot of good in
this country.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
RUGBY WORLD CUP 2011 (EMPOWERING) BILL
Instruction to Committee

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I move, That it be an
instruction to the Committee of the whole House on the Rugby World Cup 2011
(Empowering) Bill that it have the power to consider and, if it thinks fit, adopt
typescript amendments to clause 51 in the name of the Hon Trevor Mallard. That
amendment is very, very important. Although it may well be that there will be no
decision to rule it out, I think it is important that we have a belt and braces approach and
ensure that the Committee has the ability to discuss it and that there be no question of it
being ruled out. The amendment is designed to ensure there is a system put in place
whereby a Minister is unable to adjust a recommendation of the Rugby World Cup
Authority, such that he or she ends up approving something that is not otherwise
approved by that authority. In relatively simple terms, the amendment is to ensure that
there are proper checks and balances placed in the system.
I will use an example. In the case of an urgent application post-August, it would
mean that under the current legislation there could be a full hearing of an authority. We
could have witnesses, council people, and all sorts of experts—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I need a bit of clarification from the
member who is on his feet. It is my understanding that this amendment is in order;
therefore, it does not need an instruction of the House for it to be debated. It is in order.
Please acknowledge that there has been a change of presiding officer while this has been
happening. I need to understand what the member is doing, because it is my
understanding that the amendment is totally in order.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I think you are almost certainly right, Mr Assistant
Speaker, but I have also checked this. Notwithstanding the fact that it is likely to be in
order, that does not prevent this motion being moved in order to make absolutely certain
14870 Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill 27 Oct 2010
of that. There is no restriction on this motion. It is something that has been checked
through very carefully over the last 24 hours, and I have had an absolute assurance that
this motion and the next few that will come before the Committee are in order.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am just trying to think through the
precedent of what the member is actually doing. The discipline of this House is that it
lives by precedent. It would occur to me that although this step might be in order, it may
set some precedents that take the House in a direction that the House does not want to
go in. Having given the member an assurance that his amendment is in order and will be
acceptable to the Committee of the whole House, I am perplexed as to why the member
is seeking this particular course of action.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I think members on the other side of the House are
well aware of the reason for us doing this. There has been quite a lot of discussion
between members from both sides of the House on the way that this bill is being
handled. It is my understanding that although this is unusual, and may even be
unprecedented, it is within the Standing Orders. I think you are right; it is probably
identifying a loophole within the Standing Orders and could well set a precedent that
people may want to close off through a change to the Standing Orders, but that does not
mean that it can be ruled out.

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Given that you have ruled that
the amendment that the Hon Trevor Mallard has put on the Table for debate is within
order and will be debated as part of clause 51 within one of the parts of the bill this
afternoon and this evening, it seems to me that the Hon Trevor Mallard is attempting to
trifle with the House’s time and to delay our progressing to the bill. I think that is
trifling with the House’s time, and I ask you to rule that this be out of order.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Speaking to that—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I will listen to the member, then I will
respond.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Yes, sure. I think that what the member should know
is that one of the honourable roles of the Opposition is to delay. It is a longstanding
precedent. The term “filibuster” is well known in both United Kingdom and United
States politics. When bad law is being made, one of the roles of the Opposition, and one
of the very few tools of an Opposition that does not have the votes to stop particular
legislation, is to make sure that it is subject to a debate that is as extensive as is possible
in order to ensure the best possible examination of it.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Standing Order 172(1) states: “An
instruction may be given to a committee of the whole House extending or restricting its
powers …”. What the member is seeking to do is not actually extending or restricting.
He has assured me that he has done some work in the last 24 hours. I have not had the
opportunity to do that work. These are the options open to me: I can rule that the
member is having a debate that is not necessary and therefore it is out of order, I can let
the debate take its full course, or I can perhaps indicate to the House that a closure
motion might be considered at some near time in the future, when a considered decision
from the Speaker might be the best way forward. But I will allow the member to finish
his speech.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I think a problem
has now developed. It probably has been caused by the fact that there was a change of
Speaker. Mr Speaker accepted this motion.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: That is what I have done.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I am pleased to hear that, because it is very, very
important. The amendment that has been discussed is important, and by way of
extension I just want to make it very clear that in my opinion this does make an
27 Oct 2010 Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill 14871
extension because it provides both belt and braces in this arrangement. [Interruption]
Well, Peter Dunne is the person who probably understands belt and braces better than
anyone else. As I indicated earlier, the danger that we are facing is that there is a full
hearing of an authority, which takes a decision to decline a particular application. It says
that no, that should not happen. It might, for example, be the demolition of a historic
building. On the basis of the evidence, a decision is made not to demolish that historic
building. The way the bill is at the moment, and without consideration of my
amendment, a Minister could then say: “It does not matter what the judge said, it does
not matter about the fact that there was a hearing, I am going to allow my mate’s house
to be demolished.” They might have a party central, or a little “party not central” there,
for a period of time, but afterwards the section becomes available for building on, in a
way that would not otherwise be the case under current planning legislation because a
demolition would not previously have been allowed. It goes to the ability of a judge to
make a decision, and whether the House should be considering that they have the ability
to consider it.
I have another point I would like to make, and I do not think I am doing this by way
of a point of order. I think I am doing it by way of debate, although it does do it by way
of referring to the comments that you, Mr Assistant Speaker Roy, made when you were
on your feet. It is not for the Speaker to rule whether something is in or out, at the
Committee. It is a matter for the Chairman. The Speaker cannot give an assurance,
because it is not his role to give an assurance on something that he must rule on when
sitting in the Chairperson’s Chair, while he is sitting in the Speaker’s Chair. In fact, I
think there could be some question of conflict if Speakers attempted to take that sort of
approach. Although I do not think there are many men who are more honourable than
you are, as far as the House is concerned, and we do of course rely on your word, I think
we have to be very clear that the role of the Speaker is different from the role of the
Chairman, and in fact the only—

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: Is this a speech or a point of order?

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No, I think it is entirely within order. The only
circumstance where the Speaker—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I have told the member to continue with
his speech. This is not a point of order.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No. I made it clear it is not a point of order, but I am
referring to your comment, just to make it clear.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member should not litigate my
ruling.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No, I am not litigating; I am adding to it. I am saying
how much I trust you. The point I am making is that the House is unable to be given
assurances by the Speaker in this matter, because the role of the Speaker will be to
consider the matter if in fact the Chairman in error ruled it out. That then would be a
case for bringing the Speaker back to the House in order to debate the issue. I think you
could see that it would be more than slightly incongruous for you, Mr Assistant Speaker
Roy, to rule on a matter as Speaker and then to rule on it as Chairman. There is the
possibility of ruling on your own ruling as Chairman. I think that sort of approach is the
one taken in the Fijian Parliament or some other place where democracy is non-existent.
That is probably the only place where that would occur.
I want to make clear that the Labour Opposition is very firm that it is important to
have this debate. I know that my colleagues are very keen to outline to you why they
think a belt and braces approach is necessary on this particular legislation. I might say
also that because there has been a lot of debate about this matter of power within the
select committee and within the media, and because there has been a lot of discussion
14872 Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill 27 Oct 2010
about the powers in the Canterbury legislation, following the earthquake, the issue of
the limits of ministerial power are very much alive in New Zealand now. That is why it
is important that this debate is held on this subclause.
At this stage, and without going into the substance of the debate, because I think we
will get to the debate on Part 4 today or possibly after the adjournment, I say that this is
very important. I am slightly ambivalent on this argument myself, but I think there is a
certain lack of trust in the current Minister and the way that he might exercise the
powers. I think it is fair to say that the Minister has a growing reputation, which has
been highlighted by my colleague Phil Twyford, inter alia, of being involved in micro-
management across portfolios. I think it is fair to say that the fingerprints are not always
left there, but there are a few greasy marks on the piece of paper. There are signs on the
piece of paper of a Minister becoming involved in areas that he should not be involved
in. That is why we think it is important that a Minister should not get the power, without
any consideration from the Regulations Review Committee. I know that my colleague
Lianne Dalziel is involved in that committee, and certainly Chris Hipkins is involved in
that committee. If the decisions of the Minister were, for example, reviewable by a
committee of this Parliament, then I am sure—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Sounds like another amendment.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Well, I think there will be an amendment; there will
be amendment after amendment and we will take about 10 minutes to deal with each of
them, as the day goes on. But if these are not to be considered by any court, because
there is not time, and not to be considered by the Regulations Review Committee, then
it is important that the Minister not be left with this power. I want to remind the House
of what we are doing. We had someone who is an experienced judge—with a panel—
hear the evidence and make a decision, but at the end of that the Minister said that
declining that position—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: I move, That the question be now
put.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I will accept the closure, for this reason:
I think it is a novel approach and an interesting one that the Hon Trevor Mallard has
promoted. I know I do not have to give a reason why I have accepted it. I will bring
back a considered opinion. I do not believe the honourable member in his speech proved
the case that this did extend or restrict, so the question is that the question be now put.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the question be now put.

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.
Clearly the Opposition wants to put up another couple of amendments and go through
the same charade that we have just been through. In speaking, the Hon Trevor Mallard
has acknowledged that he is doing this to filibuster. He has acknowledged that that is a
tool that the Opposition has at its disposal. I bring it to your attention that this can be
used only within the rules of the House and within the Standing Orders of the House. If
the amendments that the member is seeking to have debated before we get into the
Committee stage are in fact already to be debated and have been agreed to be in order,
then I think the process of going through the charade that we have just seen in the last
10 minutes is a complete waste of the House’s time and I think you should rule them out
of order.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Firstly, I cannot prejudge what or what
may not happen. I assure all members that I will assiduously enforce the rules of this
House, as laid down by both Speakers’ Rulings and the Standing Orders.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I move that it be an
instruction to the Committee on the Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill that it
have the power to consider and, if it thinks fit, adopt the typescript amendment to
amend Subpart 3 by adding new clause 72(1)(a)(iii), set out in the name of Iain Lees-
Galloway. Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, I have indicated to the member that I
will bring back a ruling on these matters. Although the member did raise at an earlier
time that it is not for the Speaker to give an instruction or to presume what the
Committee as a whole may or may not do with amendments before the House, there is
also—and I commented on this earlier—a well laid-out set of rules that we abide by,
both in Speakers’ rulings and in the Standing Orders. It is those same rulings that the
presiding officer of the House will judge any amendment on at the time. Therefore, I am
not prepared to accept the motion that the member was about to move.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I am in a very difficult position, because we now have a Speaker ruling
differently from the senior Speaker, who ruled on the very same issue about 20 minutes
ago. Mr Assistant Speaker Roy, you know that I have considerable respect for you and
for your integrity. Certainly there is no doubt that you as Speaker—because you are
sitting in the Chair as Speaker—have the ability to make rulings, as has Mr Speaker. So
I am not debating your ability to do that; the question I ask is whether precedent applies
in this House, and whether precedents set by a Speaker on consideration not 20 minutes
ago—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Let me truncate this somewhat: the
member is out of order because Parliamentary Practice in New Zealand, by David
McGee, page 369, states: “A member may move only one instruction in relation to the
same bill.”
14874 Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill 27 Oct 2010
Therefore, I declare the House in Committee for the Rugby World Cup—

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I move, That it be an
instruction to the Committee on the Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill that it
have the power to consider and, if it thinks fit, adopt typescript amendments to clause
72 in the name of Iain Lees-Galloway.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I have said that I will bring a ruling to
the House. I realise that members want to progress this matter now, but the case really
has to be made for an extension of, or change in, the restriction to a motion, and the
rules are quite clear. Although the member earlier said that it is not for the Speaker to
give an instruction to the Chair, the rules are quite clear about whether there is an
extension or limitation. I cannot see where that occurs, so I have said that I will bring a
ruling back to the House on this matter.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. In a way, the ruling you have just given would have been fair for the previous
amendment, when there was debate about whether there was an extension or restriction.
But there is no doubt in the case of this amendment. It is a question of whether it is
within scope, and my view is that this amendment is also probably within scope. There
is no doubt whatsoever that this amendment extends the bill into an area that is not
otherwise considered, because it extends it to details of transportation options available
near the premises. My firm view is that the amendment is within the broad scope of the
bill, but, notwithstanding that it is within scope, it is an extension from the point at
which it currently sits. Again, I hope that you will continue to seek advice on this
amendment, Mr Assistant Speaker, because it is my firm opinion that it involves an
extension. It goes into an area that, although within the broad parameters of the bill, is
something that is not currently touched on. It is something that goes beyond what is in
the Sale of Liquor Act, because requirements on transportation are not part of that Act.
But in this one, having these transportation details—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I am making very serious comment to you, Mr
Assistant Speaker. I accept that as the Speaker in the Chair you would automatically
rule on the previous amendment, but it is fair to say that within this amendment there is
at least a modicum of doubt about the issue. I will repeat the comment I made before: it
cannot be for a Speaker to rule on the role of a Chair, unless by way of appeal; that
would prejudice the right of the Opposition to then take things to the Speaker later.

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: There is no modicum of doubt in
that respect. This amendment is part of the scope of the bill. It is within Part 5 and can
be debated there. The present debate is totally superfluous and is trifling with the
House’s time. I ask, Mr Assistant Speaker, that you rule against these amendments.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I think the member makes a point, which
I will pick up on. How can the Speaker possibly make a ruling when he has not been
presented with the amendments, or given the opportunity to give consideration to them,
in the same way a Chair would when amendments are tabled in the Committee of the
whole House? For that reason, since 1856 we have had a process by which the House in
Committee makes these rulings. I understand that members have raised a serious point. I
have given an assurance that these matters will be considered, and that a finding will be
brought back. For that reason, I am ruling that I am not prepared to accept debate about
instructions to the Committee in the manner in which that has been raised. I therefore
declare the House—

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Now this gets to something that I think is very serious—that is, what happens
when there is doubt in the Speaker’s mind as to his role. You have said—
27 Oct 2010 Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill 14875

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Let me answer that point.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: No, I have not finished—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Let me answer that quite clearly. There
is an option: if the House is in any way displeased or has a question, it has the right to
recall the Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: No, we don’t now—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The member will just listen; he will not
interrupt me when I am giving a ruling on a point of order. When the House is in
Committee, if members who put an amendment or a Supplementary Order Paper on the
Table feel that an inappropriate ruling has been given by the Chair, it is the right of the
Committee of the whole House to then call the Speaker back, and the Committee can do
that. I have given an assurance that there will be a ruling, so that gives us some time to
do that. It seems to me, also, that to ask the Speaker to rule on amendments that are not
tabled in front of the Speaker is a totally inappropriate way to do business; it is for that
reason amendments are tabled in the House. I therefore declare—

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I think you have missed the point. We are not asking you, as Speaker, to rule
on amendments; we are asking the House to make a decision. It is the right of members
to ask the House to make a decision. I am not asking you, as Speaker, to rule something
in or out. That is something for the Chairman to do. What I am asking the House to do,
and what my colleague is asking the House to do, is for the House to make a decision.
One of the rights of the Opposition is to put motions that are within the Standing
Orders. I do not think you have argued that these amendments are not within the
Standing Orders. I think they are—in fact, the Speaker, Dr The Rt Hon Lockwood
Smith, has accepted one amendment. You have had another come before you, Mr
Assistant Speaker, and you have quite rightly ruled. I was not aware of the McGee
ruling on the ability to move only one instruction to the Committee, but my colleague
then moved another instruction. No one is asking you, as Speaker, to rule on these
amendments. In fact, it is my view that you cannot, unless these are clearly—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Let me respond to that, because I am
bound to apply the Standing Orders. Standing Order 172(1) states: “An instruction may
be given to a committee of the whole House extending or restricting its powers …”. So I
have to rule whether the debate is in order, because that will either extend or restrict the
powers of the amendment. That is what I have to rule on, so in effect I have to rule on
the amendment. In that respect, and as a way forward, the member is saying that the
House should be able to vote on that. My thought, perhaps—because as Speaker I
should take a ruling—is that I will apply the same procedure that I applied in the first
instance, so on this occasion I will accept that procedure on this amendment, which is
that the member can take a call.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.
We have been through this process, and clearly it has been accepted on the Opposition’s
side of the House that this is simply a filibustering technique. The amendments that
have been tabled, which the Opposition is asking to be debated, are within scope, as the
member has admitted, and therefore will be debated as part of the bill in the Committee
stage. But these amendments should be ruled out of order, and we should move on to
the Committee stage.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I ask the member just to give me a
moment. Members can observe that I have taken some advice on this. I am troubled by
the fact that I have to apply Standing Order 172. I understand that these amendments are

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: The reason I have
asked the House to instruct the Committee to consider this amendment—and I accept
that it is on the bounds of the scope of the bill—is that the amendment offers an
excellent opportunity to reinforce public safety. The amendment seeks to amend clause
72, “Conditions applying to all licences”. Clause 72(1) states: “A licence granted under
this Part is, unless expressly stated otherwise, subject to the following conditions:”.
Clause 72(1)(a)(i) refers to the signage available in a licensed premises and outlines that
that sign must be “easily read by persons immediately outside the principal entrance of
the premises or within the area;”. That offers up an opportunity that this amendment
would address. I recognise and accept that it is something of an extension to the original
bill, and that is why I ask that the House consider at this point instructing the Committee
of the whole House to consider it.
The opportunity that lies here is to reinforce public safety using the signage that the
Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill will require to be in place in licensed
premises. It gives the opportunity for that signage to offer a public safety message that
patrons should seek out safe transportation options, and the options available to patrons
should be clearly made available to patrons who are enjoying the entertainment within a
licensed premises.
This is an important issue to cover in the current environment where we have a very
high blood-alcohol level tolerance in New Zealand. In fact, a number of patrons within
those establishments would get to see this message if this amendment was accepted.
They will come from countries where the blood-alcohol level tolerance is lower, and
perhaps the adjustment they will have to make on coming to New Zealand may lead to
some unsafe practices and unsafe situations on our roads, particularly in Auckland—
where a number of the games are and where there are already a number of transport
issues—but also in communities right across the country.
As I said, I accept that this is something of an extension to a clause about licensing,
the licence that is granted, and the requirement to publicly display a message that shows
that the licence under which that premises is operating is a Rugby World Cup licence
rather than the standard licence under which a premises would ordinarily operate. In
those terms, clause 72 is actually quite narrow, and in its original form it does not allow
for these sorts of safety messages to be included.
One could argue that a whole range of safety messages could be included, and that is
probably why the original clause is so narrow in its definition. But I seek the House’s
approval to consider this amendment because I think it would have a significant impact
on the community and would probably be the most important message we could get
27 Oct 2010 Rugby World Cup 2011 (Empowering) Bill 14877
through to people. I do not think, for instance, that there would be much point in putting
forward an amendment about the proximity of hospitals, the proximity of police
stations, the proximity of drug treatment facilities, or anything like that. But in all
likelihood most people will require some form of transportation so this is the most
relevant and most obvious change that could be made, and signage in the licensed
premises offers us as a Parliament the best opportunity to address an issue of
considerable debate in the public at the moment.
The public want to see Parliament taking the issue of drink-driving seriously. So,
again, even though this amendment is something of an extension in the current
environment—we have an active campaign by one of our leading national newspapers
encouraging respected members of the public and parliamentarians to get on board with
the drink-driving message, to consider safe options for transportation, and to be aware
of the options that are available to them—it is entirely relevant and appropriate in this
bill.
We know that the Rugby World Cup as a tournament, as an event, will offer up far
more opportunities for people to go out and enjoy themselves, probably become
intoxicated, and get themselves into a position where knowledge about the options in
terms of transport available to them becomes very, very important in terms of public
safety and the safety of the wider community—including those who choose not to be in
the licensed premises, those who are simply out on the road, undertaking business that
has nothing to do with the Rugby World Cup whatsoever. Those people will be very
concerned—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: What are their names?

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I could list them—but those members of the public will
be very concerned that although the majority of the impacts are positive, there is the
opportunity for some of those impacts on our communities to be negative. This
amendment would address and mitigate one of the potentially negative impacts that the
Rugby World Cup could have in the wider community.
It is not currently incumbent on the licensee who has to display the sign referred to in
clause 72(1)(a)(i) and (ii) to make available to patrons information about transportation
options. It is a requirement that they have low alcoholic drinks, non-alcoholic drinks,
and food, and that those things are all clearly on display. However, although there is a
requirement to ensure that transport options are available, there is no requirement in the
bill at the moment to make sure that those options are clearly on display and that that
information is available to patrons. So by recommending to the Committee of the whole
House that this amendment be considered, the House is dealing with an issue not
currently provided for in the bill.
All the other measures to mitigate the potential harms of alcohol will be on display
and available to patrons, but there is no provision for this measure—which is probably
the most relevant and would have the most impact—to be on display. I accept and
acknowledge that the amendment is probably on the outer limits in terms of the scope of
the bill, but I ask that the House consider this motion, vote in favour of it, and direct the
Committee of the whole House to consider the amendment in the interests of public
safety.
